    <div class="mds-legacy-col-12 mds-legacy-col-md-6" style="background:#eef6ff; padding:8px">Half</div>

## Customize

Override defaults before importing:

```scss
$base-unit: 0.25rem; // 4px at 16px root
$gutter: 0.5rem;     // 8px at 16px root
$columns: 12;
@use '../styles/grid' as *;
```

Adjust `$breakpoints` and `$container-max` for different responsive behavior.

### Runtime tuning via CSS variables

You can tune grid gaps and min column width at runtime per section without recompiling Sass:

```html
<div class="mds-legacy-row" style="--mds-grid-gap: 12px">…</div>
<div class="mds-legacy-row-auto" style="--mds-grid-col-min: 240px">…</div>
```

This is helpful for special layouts (e.g., tighter gaps on dense dashboards) while keeping defaults aligned to the design tokens.

## Phase 1 Enhancements: Advanced Grid Features

### Non-12-Column Grids

Use `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-{N}` to create grids with any column count (not just 12):

```html
<div class="mds-legacy-grid-cols-5 mds-legacy-gap-4">
  <div>1</div><div>2</div><div>3</div><div>4</div><div>5</div>
</div>
```

  <div style={{ background:'#c7edff', padding:8, textAlign:'center' }}>2</div>
  <div style={{ background:'#e5edf4', padding:8, textAlign:'center' }}>3</div>
  <div style={{ background:'#c7edff', padding:8, textAlign:'center' }}>4</div>

</div>

**Responsive**: `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-1 .mds-legacy-grid-cols-md-3 .mds-legacy-grid-cols-lg-5` stacks on mobile, 3 cols on tablet, 5 cols on desktop.

</div>

### Responsive Visibility

**Hide at specific breakpoints**: `.mds-legacy-hidden-xs`, `.mds-legacy-hidden-md`, `.mds-legacy-hidden-lg`

**Show only at breakpoints**: `.mds-legacy-visible-md` (only visible on tablets)

```html
<div class="mds-legacy-hidden-xs">Hidden on mobile</div>
<div class="mds-legacy-visible-lg">Only visible on large screens</div>
```

## Complete Utility Reference

### Column Spanning
- `.mds-legacy-col-1` to `.mds-legacy-col-12` • `.mds-legacy-col-{bp}-{N}` • `.mds-legacy-col-auto`

### Grid Template Columns
- `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-1` to `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-12` • `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-{bp}-{N}`
- Presets: `.mds-legacy-grid-auto-fit-{xs|sm|md|lg}`, `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-sidebar`, `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-two-thirds`

### Row Spanning
- `.mds-legacy-row-span-1` to `.mds-legacy-row-span-6` • `.mds-legacy-row-span-full` • `.mds-legacy-row-span-{bp}-{N}`

### Grid Rows
- `.mds-legacy-grid-rows-1` to `.mds-legacy-grid-rows-6` • `.mds-legacy-grid-rows-{bp}-{N}`

### Gaps
- Standard: `.mds-legacy-gap-0`, `.mds-legacy-gap-1` (4px), `.mds-legacy-gap-2` (8px), `.mds-legacy-gap-4` (16px), `.mds-legacy-gap-8` (32px)
- Extended: `.mds-legacy-gap-9` (36px), `.mds-legacy-gap-12` (48px), `.mds-legacy-gap-16` (64px), `.mds-legacy-gap-20` (80px), `.mds-legacy-gap-24` (96px)
- Directional: `.mds-legacy-gap-x-{N}`, `.mds-legacy-gap-y-{N}`, `.mds-legacy-gx-{N}`, `.mds-legacy-gy-{N}`
- Responsive: `.mds-legacy-gap-{bp}-{N}`

### Alignment
- Items: `.mds-legacy-align-{start|center|end}`, `.mds-legacy-justify-{start|center|end}`
- Content: `.mds-legacy-content-align-{start|center|end|between|around|evenly}`
- Place: `.mds-legacy-place-items-{start|center|end|stretch}`, `.mds-legacy-place-content-{start|center|end|between}`

### Grid Flow
- `.mds-legacy-grid-flow-row`, `.mds-legacy-grid-flow-col`, `.mds-legacy-grid-flow-dense`

### Visibility
- `.mds-legacy-hidden-{xs|sm|md|lg|xl}` • `.mds-legacy-visible-{xs|sm|md|lg|xl}`

### Offsets
- `.mds-legacy-offset-1` to `.mds-legacy-offset-11` • `.mds-legacy-offset-{bp}-{N}`

### Ordering (Bootstrap-inspired)
- `.mds-legacy-order-0` to `.mds-legacy-order-12` • `.mds-legacy-order-first` • `.mds-legacy-order-last`
- Responsive: `.mds-legacy-order-{bp}-{N}`, `.mds-legacy-order-{bp}-first`, `.mds-legacy-order-{bp}-last`

## Bootstrap-Inspired Patterns

### Equal-Width Columns (Auto-Layout)

Use `.mds-legacy-col` (no number) for equal-width columns:

  <div class="mds-legacy-col">2 of 2</div>
</div>

  <div class="mds-legacy-col">1 of 3</div>
  <div class="mds-legacy-col">2 of 3</div>
  <div class="mds-legacy-col">3 of 3</div>
</div>

  <div class="mds-legacy-col mds-legacy-order-2">Third in DOM (order: 2)</div>

## Complete Utility Reference

<div style={{ color: '#1a1a1a', background: 'transparent' }}>

### Column Classes

| Class | Description | Responsive Variants |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| `.mds-legacy-col-{1-12}` | Span N columns out of 12 | `.mds-legacy-col-{bp}-{1-12}` |
| `.mds-legacy-col` | Equal-width auto column (Bootstrap-style) | `.mds-legacy-col-{bp}` |
| `.mds-legacy-col-auto` | Size to content | `.mds-legacy-col-{bp}-auto` |

**Example:** `.mds-legacy-col-6 .mds-legacy-col-md-4 .mds-legacy-col-lg-3` → 50% mobile → 33% tablet → 25% desktop

### Grid Layout Classes

| Class | Description | Responsive Variants |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-{1-12}` | Create N-column grid | `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-{bp}-{1-12}` |
| `.mds-legacy-grid-rows-{1-6}` | Create N-row grid | `.mds-legacy-grid-rows-{bp}-{1-6}` |
| `.mds-legacy-grid-auto-fit-{xs\|sm\|md\|lg}` | Auto-fit columns at min size (150/200/300/400px) | `.mds-legacy-grid-auto-fit-{bp}-{size}` |
| `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-sidebar` | Fixed 250px + flexible column | — |
| `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-two-thirds` | 2fr + 1fr asymmetric layout | — |

**Example:** `.mds-legacy-grid-cols-2 .mds-legacy-grid-cols-md-4` → 2 columns mobile → 4 columns tablet

### Row & Column Spanning

| Class | Description | Responsive Variants |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| `.mds-legacy-row-span-{1-6}` | Span N rows | `.mds-legacy-row-span-{bp}-{1-6}` |
| `.mds-legacy-row-span-full` | Span all rows | `.mds-legacy-row-span-{bp}-full` |
| `.mds-legacy-col-span-{1-12}` | Span N columns | `.mds-legacy-col-span-{bp}-{1-12}` |
| `.mds-legacy-col-span-full` | Span all columns | `.mds-legacy-col-span-{bp}-full` |

**Example:** `.mds-legacy-row-span-2` makes a widget span 2 rows in dashboard layouts

### Gap & Spacing

| Class | Description | Responsive Variants |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| `.mds-legacy-gap-{0-8}` | Gap from 0-32px (4px scale) | `.mds-legacy-gap-{bp}-{0-8}` |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-{9-24}` | Extended gaps 36-96px | `.mds-legacy-gap-{bp}-{9-24}` |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-x-{0-24}` | Horizontal gap only | `.mds-legacy-gap-x-{bp}-{0-24}` |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-y-{0-24}` | Vertical gap only | `.mds-legacy-gap-y-{bp}-{0-24}` |
| `.mds-legacy-no-gutters` | Remove all gaps | — |

**Gap Scale:** 0, 4px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 20px, 24px, 28px, 32px, 36px, 40px, 48px, 56px, 64px, 72px, 80px, 88px, 96px

### Ordering

| Class | Description | Responsive Variants |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| `.mds-legacy-order-{0-12}` | Set explicit order | `.mds-legacy-order-{bp}-{0-12}` |
| `.mds-legacy-order-first` | Move to start (-1) | `.mds-legacy-order-{bp}-first` |
| `.mds-legacy-order-last` | Move to end (13) | `.mds-legacy-order-{bp}-last` |

**Example:** `.mds-legacy-order-2 .mds-legacy-order-md-1` → Order 2 on mobile → Order 1 on tablet

### Alignment & Justification

| Class | Description | Responsive Variants |
|-------|-------------|---------------------|
| `.mds-legacy-items-start\|center\|end\|baseline\|stretch` | Align items (cross-axis) | `.mds-legacy-items-{bp}-{value}` |
| `.mds-legacy-justify-start\|center\|end\|between\|around\|evenly` | Justify content (main-axis) | `.mds-legacy-justify-{bp}-{value}` |
| `.mds-legacy-place-items-{start\|center\|end\|stretch}` | Combined item placement | `.mds-legacy-place-items-{bp}-{value}` |
| `.mds-legacy-place-content-{start\|center\|end\|between\|around\|evenly}` | Combined content placement | `.mds-legacy-place-content-{bp}-{value}` |

|-------|-------------|

The grid system has been significantly enhanced with modern enterprise features:

### ⭐ New in Grid 2.0

- **XXL Breakpoint** (1540px): Ultra-wide screen support
- **Extended Spacing**: `.mds-legacy-gap-28` (112px), `.mds-legacy-gap-32` (128px) for enterprise layouts  
- **Aspect Ratio Utilities**: `.mds-legacy-aspect-video`, `.mds-legacy-aspect-square`, `.mds-legacy-aspect-4-3`, etc.
- **Subgrid Support**: Future-ready alignment with `.mds-legacy-subgrid-cols`, `.mds-legacy-subgrid-rows`

## Customization

### SCSS Variables

```scss
// Override in your styles
$grid-columns: 12;        // Total columns
$gutter: 8px;             // Default gap
$grid-breakpoints: (
  xs: 0,
  sm: 576px,
  md: 768px,
  lg: 1024px,
  xl: 1200px,
  xxl: 1540px
);
```

### CSS Custom Properties

```css
/* Runtime customization */
.custom-grid {
  --mds-grid-gap: 24px;  /* Custom gap per instance */
}
```

## Tips & Best Practices

**Mobile-First Approach**
- Start with mobile layout (`.mds-legacy-col-12`), then add breakpoints
- Example: `.mds-legacy-col-12 .mds-legacy-col-md-6 .mds-legacy-col-lg-4` → Stack → 2 cols → 3 cols

**Performance**
- Use `.mds-legacy-grid-auto-fit-md` for responsive cards instead of multiple breakpoints
- Prefer `.mds-legacy-col` for equal-width layouts (simpler than `.mds-legacy-col-{1-12}`)

**Accessibility**
- Use `.mds-legacy-order-*` to reorder visually, but keep DOM order logical for screen readers
- Ensure sufficient color contrast in custom backgrounds

**Debugging**
- Add borders temporarily: `.mds-legacy-row { border: 2px solid red; } .mds-legacy-col { border: 1px solid blue; }`
- Use browser DevTools Grid Inspector to visualize layout

### 🎯 Breakpoint Decision Tree

**Which breakpoint to use?**
- `xs` (0px): **Always start here** - mobile-first
- `sm` (600px): Large phones in landscape, small tablets
- `md` (900px): Tablets in portrait, small laptops  
- `lg` (1024px): Laptops, desktops
- `xl` (1200px): Large desktops, external monitors
- **`xxl` (1540px): Ultra-wide monitors, enterprise dashboards**

**Common responsive patterns:**
- **Two-column**: `.mds-legacy-col-12 .mds-legacy-col-md-8` + `.mds-legacy-col-12 .mds-legacy-col-md-4`
- **Three-column**: `.mds-legacy-col-12 .mds-legacy-col-md-6 .mds-legacy-col-lg-4`
- **Four-column**: `.mds-legacy-col-12 .mds-legacy-col-md-6 .mds-legacy-col-lg-4 .mds-legacy-col-xl-3`
- **🆕 Ultra-wide**: `.mds-legacy-col-xxl-3 .mds-legacy-col-xl-4 .mds-legacy-col-lg-6 .mds-legacy-col-md-12`

### 📏 Spacing Scale Quick Reference

| Class | Value | When to Use |
|-------|-------|-------------|
| `.mds-legacy-gap-1` | 4px | Tight content, buttons |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-2` | 8px | Form fields, list items |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-3` | 12px | Card padding, small gaps |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-4` | 16px | **Most common - general spacing** |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-6` | 24px | Section spacing, large cards |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-8` | 32px | Component spacing |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-12` | 48px | Large section gaps |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-16` | 64px | Major section divisions |
| `.mds-legacy-gap-24` | 96px | Page-level spacing |
| **🆕 `.mds-legacy-gap-28`** | **112px** | **Enterprise section spacing** |
| **🆕 `.mds-legacy-gap-32`** | **128px** | **Maximum ultra-wide spacing** |

### 🖼 Aspect Ratios by Use Case

| Class | Ratio | Perfect For | Example |
|-------|-------|-------------|---------|
| `.mds-legacy-aspect-square` | 1:1 | Profile images, avatars, icons | `<div class="mds-legacy-aspect-square"><img src="avatar.jpg"></div>` |
| `.mds-legacy-aspect-video` | 16:9 | Videos, hero images | `<div class="mds-legacy-aspect-video"><video>...</video></div>` |
| `.mds-legacy-aspect-4-3` | 4:3 | Traditional photos | `<div class="mds-legacy-aspect-4-3"><img src="photo.jpg"></div>` |
| `.mds-legacy-aspect-3-2` | 3:2 | Modern photography | `<div class="mds-legacy-aspect-3-2"><img src="landscape.jpg"></div>` |
| `.mds-legacy-aspect-21-9` | 21:9 | Ultra-wide content | `<div class="mds-legacy-aspect-21-9">Ultra-wide banner</div>` |
| `.mds-legacy-aspect-auto` | auto | Reset to natural size | `<div class="mds-legacy-aspect-auto">Natural dimensions</div>` |

### 🔄 Responsive Variants Cheat Sheet

**Pattern**: `.{utility}-{breakpoint}-{value}`

```html
<!-- Responsive columns -->
.col-12         <!-- All screens: 12 columns (100%) -->
.col-sm-6       <!-- Small+: 6 columns (50%) -->  
.col-md-4       <!-- Medium+: 4 columns (33%) -->
.col-lg-3       <!-- Large+: 3 columns (25%) -->
.col-xl-2       <!-- XL+: 2 columns (16%) -->
.col-xxl-1      <!-- XXL+: 1 column (8%) -->

<!-- Responsive gaps -->
.gap-4          <!-- All screens: 16px gap -->
.gap-md-6       <!-- Medium+: 24px gap -->
.gap-lg-8       <!-- Large+: 32px gap -->
.gap-xl-12      <!-- XL+: 48px gap -->
.gap-xxl-16     <!-- XXL+: 64px gap -->

<!-- Responsive aspect ratios -->
.aspect-square      <!-- All screens: 1:1 -->
.aspect-md-video    <!-- Medium+: 16:9 -->
.aspect-lg-4-3      <!-- Large+: 4:3 -->

<!-- Responsive subgrid -->
.subgrid-cols          <!-- All screens: inherit columns -->
.subgrid-lg-rows       <!-- Large+: inherit rows -->
.subgrid-xxl-both      <!-- XXL+: inherit both -->
```

### ⚡ Performance Tips

**Fastest Grid Patterns:**
1. **`.mds-legacy-container` + `.mds-legacy-row` + `.mds-legacy-col-*`** - Most optimized
2. **`.mds-legacy-grid-auto-fit-md`** - Auto-responsive without media queries
3. **`.mds-legacy-col` (no number)** - Equal-width, minimal CSS

**Avoid These:**
- ❌ Nested `.mds-legacy-container` inside `.mds-legacy-container`
- ❌ Using `.mds-legacy-row` without `.mds-legacy-col-*` children
- ❌ Mixing flexbox and grid utilities on same element

**With MUI Components:**

### 🔧 Troubleshooting Common Issues

**Grid Not Working?**
1. ✅ Check if `.mds-legacy-row` has `.mds-legacy-col-*` children
2. ✅ Verify total columns don't exceed 12
3. ✅ Ensure no typos in class names
4. ✅ Check responsive order with DevTools

**Layout Breaking on Mobile?**
1. ✅ Use `.mds-legacy-col-12` for mobile-first
2. ✅ Test with DevTools mobile view  
3. ✅ Check if content overflow is hidden
4. ✅ Verify touch-friendly tap targets (44px minimum)

**XXL Not Working?**
1. ✅ Check viewport is actually 1540px+
2. ✅ Verify no conflicting CSS
3. ✅ Test with browser zoom at 100%
4. ✅ Check if other utilities override

### 📱 Browser Support Matrix

| Feature | Chrome | Firefox | Safari | Edge | Mobile |
|---------|--------|---------|--------|------|--------|
| Grid System | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| XXL Breakpoint | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Aspect Ratios | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Subgrid** | 🔄 | ✅ | ✅ | 🔄 | 🔄 |
| Container Queries | ✅ | 🔄 | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

**Legend:** ✅ Full support, 🔄 Partial/Coming soon

---

## 🚀 Migration & Upgrade Path

### From Previous Grid Version

**✅ Backward Compatible:**
- All existing `.mds-legacy-col-*`, `.mds-legacy-gap-*` classes work unchanged
- All breakpoints `xs` through `xl` unchanged  
- Container behavior identical

**🆕 New Features to Adopt:**
```scss
// 1. Add XXL breakpoint support
.metric-card {
  @extend .mds-legacy-col-12, .mds-legacy-col-md-6, .mds-legacy-col-lg-4, .mds-legacy-col-xl-3, .mds-legacy-col-xxl-2;
}

// 2. Use extended spacing for enterprise layouts  
.dashboard-section {
  @extend .mds-legacy-gap-xxl-32, .mds-legacy-gap-xl-24, .mds-legacy-gap-lg-16, .mds-legacy-gap-8;
}

// 3. Replace custom aspect ratio CSS
.video-container {
  @extend .mds-legacy-aspect-video; // Instead of padding-bottom: 56.25%
}

// 4. Prepare for subgrid (progressive enhancement)
.card-grid {
  @extend .mds-legacy-row, .mds-legacy-gap-6;
  grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; // Ready for subgrid
  
  .card {
    @extend .mds-legacy-col-4, .mds-legacy-subgrid-rows; // Works when supported
  }
}
```

# Elevation

Elevation communicates layering, interactivity and focus. We keep a compact shadow scale to reduce visual noise.

<div style={{
  background: '#fff3e0',
  padding: '16px 20px',
  borderRadius: '8px',
  marginBottom: '24px',
  border: '1px solid #ffcc80'
}}>
  <strong>Is this Tailwind?</strong> No — the scale below is MDS's own (<code>src/shadows.ts</code>, 6 levels, each with a
  documented semantic usage), not Tailwind's default shadow scale (<code>shadow-sm</code>, <code>shadow-md</code>,
  <code>shadow-lg</code>, <code>shadow-xl</code>, <code>shadow-2xl</code>). Unlike grid, this hasn't
  been reconciled yet: several <code>src/components/ui</code> components (button, chart, context-menu, dialog,
  dropdown-menu, input, input-group, menubar, message-scroller, questionnaire, select, sheet, stat-card, textarea, toast)
  currently reach for Tailwind's bare shadow utilities directly instead of this scale — a real, undocumented
  split worth reconciling later, not addressed on this page yet.
</div>

## Scale

<ElevationGrid />

## Light vs Dark Comparison

Visual parity of elevation levels across themes. Future iterations may tune shadow opacity per theme to reduce glow in dark mode.

<ElevationCompare />

## Guidelines

- Prefer the lowest possible level that provides adequate separation.
- Use level 0 for nested containers and cards on tinted backgrounds.
- Level 1–2 for standard cards and interactive surfaces.
- Level 3 for transient layers like menus, popovers.
- Level 4 for dialogs and blocking UI.
- Level 5 reserved for critical overlays (rare).

## Accessibility & Theming
Always ensure sufficient contrast between elevated surface and the background. In dark mode, reduce shadow spread intensity; consider using subtle border + low alpha shadow combination.

# Choosing a table Three components render tabular data, and the difference between two of...
import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Foundations/Choosing a table" />

# Choosing a table

Three components render tabular data, and the difference between two of them is
**not** what they can do. Reading their story lists side by side will not tell you
which to reach for, so this page does.

<div style={{ display: 'grid', gap: 16, gridTemplateColumns: 'repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr))', margin: '24px 0' }}>
  <div style={{ border: '1px solid var(--role-border-subtle, #e3e3e3)', borderRadius: 12, padding: 16 }}>
    <h3 style={{ margin: '0 0 8px' }}><code>Table</code></h3>
    <p style={{ margin: 0, fontSize: 14 }}>
      A simple, read-oriented table. Its own implementation — no TanStack, no shared
      engine.
    </p>
    <p style={{ margin: '8px 0 0', fontSize: 13, opacity: 0.75 }}>
      Prefer <code>DataTable</code> for new work. See “Table’s future” below.
    </p>
  </div>
  <div style={{ border: '1px solid var(--role-border-subtle, #e3e3e3)', borderRadius: 12, padding: 16 }}>
    <h3 style={{ margin: '0 0 8px' }}><code>DataTable</code></h3>
    <p style={{ margin: 0, fontSize: 14 }}>
      The default choice. Pass props, get a table. Every capability the grid has is
      reachable through an <code>enable*</code> prop.
    </p>
  </div>
  <div style={{ border: '1px solid var(--role-border-subtle, #e3e3e3)', borderRadius: 12, padding: 16 }}>
    <h3 style={{ margin: '0 0 8px' }}><code>DataGrid</code></h3>
    <p style={{ margin: 0, fontSize: 14 }}>
      The same engine, composed. Reach for it when <strong>you need the table
      instance</strong> — not when you need more features.
    </p>
  </div>
</div>

## The thing that confuses everyone

**`DataTable` and `DataGrid` are the same component with two API shapes.**

`DataTable` imports `DataGrid` and renders it. It is a preset, not a lesser tier.
There is no capability in one that is missing from the other — sorting, filtering,
selection, pinning, reordering, resizing, virtualization, inline editing, cell
ranges and clipboard are all available either way.

So the question is never *“do I need more power?”*. It is:

> **Does anything outside the table need to read or drive its state?**

| | `DataTable` | `DataGrid` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| API | ~28 props | composed children |
| Who owns the table instance | the component | **you** |
| Read selection / filters / sorting directly | no — only via callbacks | yes |
| Reorder, replace or omit parts | no | yes |
| Capabilities | identical | identical |

**Use `DataTable`** unless one of these is true:

- a toolbar, header or side panel outside the table needs to read its state;
- you need to drive the table from elsewhere (a saved view, a URL, another control);
- you need to replace a part, or leave one out;
- you want the toolbar somewhere other than above the table.

**Then use `DataGrid`**, and see its `ConsumerOwnedState` story — that one story is the
entire reason this API exists.

## Reading the stories

Because the two share an engine, several stories necessarily look alike. What each
set is *for*:

- **`Components/DataTable`** — the preset. Props in, table out. This is where
  capabilities are demonstrated: selection, column visibility, server pagination,
  inline editing, the state variants.
- **`Components/DataGrid`** — composition. How the parts assemble, and what becomes
  possible once you hold the instance.
- **`Components/Table`** — the simple table. Nothing here is unique to it.

A story appearing in both places is showing the same behaviour through two APIs, not
two behaviours.

## Table’s future

`Table` shares no code with the other two. Every fix has to be made twice, and its
capabilities were deliberately ported to the grid so it could be retired — see the
`capabilities ported from table.tsx` suite in `data-grid-edges.test.tsx`.

**It is now deprecated** — since 0.7.0, removed after 0.8.0 (2026-12-23). The last
capability it had that the grid lacked was an opening sort, now `initialSorting`, and as
of 2026-09-26 it has **zero consumers**: the four app surfaces and the Figma Code Connect
mapping all point at `DataTable`.

It is not deleted yet, deliberately. `Table` has been a published export since 0.6.0 while
its deprecation reads *"since 0.7.0"* — a version that has never shipped — so no consumer
has actually been warned. Removing it now would break an API nobody was told about. It
goes when 0.7.0 has carried the warning and 0.8.0 arrives.

### The markup primitives

The tier `Table` was pretending to be. `TableHeader`, `TableBody`, `TableFooter`,
`TableRow`, `TableHead`, `TableCell` and `TableCaption` are exported now; the `Table` root
itself joins them when the legacy engine is removed, because it currently owns that name.

```tsx
<table>
  <TableHeader>
    <TableRow><TableHead>Policy</TableHead><TableHead>Premium</TableHead></TableRow>
  </TableHeader>
  <TableBody>
    <TableRow><TableCell>Commercial Auto</TableCell><TableCell>$12,400</TableCell></TableRow>
  </TableBody>
</table>
```

They carry this system's styling and nothing else — no state, no sorting, no pagination.
`DataGrid` is their first consumer, which is what keeps them honest: header height, cell
padding and the type scale are defined there once rather than restated in the grid.

The evidence that this was overdue: the ambiguous `aria-label="Select all rows"` and the
positional `Select row N` were both fixed on the grid, and both still sit in `table.tsx`,
because nothing connects the two implementations. It also has zero tests, against roughly
ninety on the grid.

Migrating:

| `Table` | `DataTable` |
| --- | --- |
| `variant="bordered"` | the default — `DataGridContainer` draws it |
| `variant="borderless"` | `<DataGridContainer border={false}>` |
| `variant="striped"` | `striped` |
| `variant="compact"` / `size` | `defaultDensity="compact"` |
| `defaultSortColumn` + `defaultSortDirection` | `initialSorting={[{ id, desc }]}` |
| `emptyMessage` | `emptyState` |
| `onRowSelect` | `enableRowSelection` + `onSelectionChange` |

Two props do **not** carry over, deliberately: `hoverable={false}` (a row you can interact
with should say so) and `onSort` (with `DataGrid` you hold the instance and can read
sorting directly, which is strictly more capable than a callback).

## When not to use a table at all

Tables exist so people can compare the same attributes across many records. If that
is not the task, something else is usually better:

- one record at a time → a detail view;
- few comparable attributes → a list or cards;
- hierarchy matters more than comparison → a tree;
- trend matters more than values → a chart.

# Contrast Quality This page centralizes the automated contrast governance for the design ...
import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';
import { ContrastStatus } from './_components/ContrastStatus';

<Meta title="Foundations/Contrast" />

# Contrast Quality

<ContrastStatus />

This page centralizes the automated contrast governance for the design system.

## What The Badge Means
The badge reflects the current result of the local WCAG contrast audit across both light and dark modes:
- PASS: All required (non-informational) token pairs meet or exceed their ratio thresholds.
- FAIL: One or more required pairs fall below threshold (investigate before merging).
- INFO: One or more informational pairs were included (optional) and may not meet ratios; these do not fail CI unless explicitly enforced.

Informational pairs are intentionally unrealistic or context-dependent (e.g., accent-on-surface where that combination is never directly rendered as text/background in a real component) but tracked for visibility.

## Regenerating The Badge
```bash
npm run tokens:contrast:badge
```
Generates / updates two artifacts at repo root:
- `contrast-badge.svg` (display asset)
- `contrast-badge.json` (structured badge payload)

## Full Contrast Report
Produce a structured JSON report of every pair in all modes:
```bash
npm run tokens:contrast:json > contrast-report.json
```
Or with informational pairs expanded in terminal output:
```bash
npm run tokens:contrast:info
```

## Typical Workflow
1. Adjust primitive or semantic tokens.
2. Run `npm run tokens:check` (builds, validates, contrast checks).
3. If a contrast failure appears, tweak semantic dark overrides (preferred) or primitives (only if widely beneficial).
4. Regenerate badge if merging a meaningful change.

## CI Behavior
The GitHub Action consumes the JSON report and annotates failures. Informational pairs are excluded unless the flag `--include-informational` is added. The workflow can be extended later to comment on PRs with a diff summary.

## Future Enhancements (Planned)
- Per-token historical trend (sparkline) by persisting past reports.
- PR comment summarizing changed contrast statuses.
- Live interactive contrast playground (token picker + backgrounds).

## Role-Level Contrast (Full Enforcement)
Role contrast is validated in `roles.contrast.test.ts`. All tracked role foreground/background pairs now meet or exceed required ratios in both light and dark modes.

Current status:
- 100% of role pairs enforced (0 monitored)
- Interactive primary (onAccent text) and all status pairs were the final items promoted after dark mode adjustments

Governance implications:
- Any regression in required contrast now fails tests, the governance script (`npm run governance:ci`), and CI.
- To introduce a new pair iteratively, you can temporarily reintroduce a monitored section in the test and governance script—but the default expectation is full enforcement.

If future visual refinements create temporary contrast dips, prefer adjusting dark overrides rapidly rather than reclassifying pairs as monitored.

---

# Documentation Guidelines This page defines how we write and structure design system docu...
import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Foundations/Documentation-Guidelines" />

# Documentation Guidelines

This page defines how we write and structure design system documentation (MDX + Autodocs).

## Core Principles
1. Single source of truth: component APIs live in CSF stories (Autodocs); conceptual & foundational narratives live in MDX.
2. Keep MDX mostly narrative; move logic & rendering complexity into imported React helper components.
3. Prefer semantic clarity over visual cleverness—docs should be skimmable and linkable.

## Markdown / MDX Standard
We follow **GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM)** where compatible with MDX.

Reference spec: https://github.github.com/gfm/

### Supported GFM Features We Use
- Tables (for tokens, comparison, matrices).
- Fenced code blocks with language hints (` ```tsx ` etc.).
- Autolinks & inline code spans.
- Task lists (only in contributor docs / not rendered inside Storybook nav yet) for internal checklists.

### Features to Avoid or Use Sparingly
- Raw HTML tags (e.g. `<button>`) inside prose—prefer backticks (`button`) to avoid parse edge cases.
- Deep nested lists (harder to scan). Flatten content or break into new sections.
- Excessive inline styling; use components or theme tokens.

## MDX Structure Rules
- Each MDX page must export a single `meta` object at the top with a `title`.
- Heading order: one `#` (title) then `##` level sections. Do not skip levels.
- Place future work / TODO notes in an italic block at bottom (`_Future: ..._`).
- Import helper components from `./_components/*` or root tokens (e.g. `../spacing`).
- Keep frontmatter out (not needed with Storybook’s indexer).

## Autodocs Integration
For components:
1. Add `tags: ['autodocs']` in the CSF default export (if you want the autogenerated docs tab).
2. Our authored MDX pages use a Controls‑only approach (no separate `ArgsTable` / `ArgTypes` blocks) because Controls already surfaces prop name, description, default & live editing.
3. Use the shared `<ApiSection />` component instead of manually placing `<Controls />` and variant `<Story />` blocks.
4. Only create a bespoke MDX page if narrative complexity (patterns, anti‑patterns, accessibility guidance) justifies it.

### ApiSection Usage Pattern
```mdx
// import { Story } from '@storybook/blocks';
// import * as ButtonStories from '../../components/Button/Button.stories';
// import { ApiSection } from '../Components/ApiSection';

// export const meta = { title: 'Components/Button' };

## Examples
<Story of={ButtonStories.Primary} />
<Story of={ButtonStories.Secondary} />

## Playground
<ApiSection primary={ButtonStories.Primary} variants={[ButtonStories.Secondary, ButtonStories.Danger]} />
```
Guidelines:
- Pass the primary (most representative) story to `primary`.
- List only meaningful variant stories in `variants` (avoid noise like trivial arg permutations).
- Omit `variants` if the component has a single canonical presentation.

## Referencing Stories in MDX
Prefer module/story references over string IDs:
`<Story of={ButtonStories.Primary} />` instead of `<Story id="components-button--primary" />`.
IDs are brittle during renames; story exports are refactor‑safe.

## Design Tokens
Tokens are code-first. MDX should render them dynamically so docs always match code (`ColorSwatches`, `TypographyTable`, `ElevationGrid`). Avoid copying values manually into tables.

## Accessibility Content
When documenting patterns, prefer: guidance list → example → counter-example (DO / DON’T) — plan a small `<DoDont />` block component for future expansion.

## Linting & Quality (Planned)
- Add a docs lint script to enforce: single `<Meta>`, no `<Story id=...>`, no deprecated `ArgsTable` / `ArgTypes` usage, heading depth.
- Visual regression (Chromatic) will track design token component diffs.

## Changelog Discipline
Any breaking token rename or removal must: (1) update token source file, (2) update affected MDX narrative, (3) annotate change in `CHANGELOG.md` under a Docs section.

## Quick Author Checklist
- [ ] File name ordered (e.g. `70-NewTopic.mdx`).
- [ ] Single `<Meta>`.
- [ ] Uses `<ApiSection>` (no manual `<Controls>` unless a special case).
- [ ] No raw HTML tags in prose.
- [ ] Logic refactored to helper component if > ~10 lines.
- [ ] Uses story `of={...}` references, not `id=`.
- [ ] Tokens pulled from source, not hard-coded.
- [ ] Future TODO (if applicable) placed at bottom.

# Testing Everything a developer needs to run this repo's tests — locally, from inside Sto...
import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Foundations/Testing" />

# Testing

Everything a developer needs to run this repo's tests — locally, from inside Storybook itself, and in CI — in one place. The full command reference also lives in the README's Testing section; this page is the fuller walkthrough, including the Storybook-UI paths that don't have a CLI equivalent.

## The two test suites

`vitest.config.ts` defines two Vitest **projects** — both run whenever you run "the tests," but they test different things in different environments:

| Project | Environment | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `unit` | jsdom | Component behavior, hooks, utilities — anything under `src/__tests__/`, `*.unit.test.ts(x)`, `src/components/**/*.test.tsx`, `src/utils/**/*.test.tsx` |
| `storybook` | Real Chromium, via Playwright (`@storybook/addon-vitest`) | Every `.stories.tsx` file in the repo, rendered for real — not jsdom, not a mock DOM |

The `storybook` project is the important one to understand if you're used to writing separate test files: **you don't write a test for a story — the story *is* the test.** Any `.stories.tsx` you add is automatically picked up and rendered as a real browser test with zero extra setup. Interaction tests (`play` functions) run as part of the same pass.

## Running tests

```bash
npm test                              # both projects
npm run test:watch                    # both projects, watch mode
npx vitest run --project unit         # just the unit suite
npx vitest run --project storybook    # just the stories, as real browser tests
```

**Cold-cache note:** the first `storybook`-project run after clearing `node_modules/.cache/storybook` can show transient "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module" failures — Vite's dependency pre-bundling racing under load, not a real failure. A second run passes cleanly. If you hit this in CI, retry once or add a cache-warming step first.

## Coverage

Coverage tells you which lines of your actual source code your tests exercised — and, more usefully, which they *didn't*.

```bash
npm run test:coverage              # both projects combined — one number per file
npm run test:coverage:storybook    # storybook project only — coverage from stories alone
```

The distinction matters: `test:coverage` mixes together whatever a story touched *and* whatever a plain unit test touched into a single per-file percentage. If you specifically want to know "how much of this component's code do its stories alone exercise" — useful for a policy like "every component needs a story that covers most of it" — use the `:storybook` variant instead; the combined number can't isolate that.

### From inside Storybook itself

You don't need the CLI for this. In Storybook's sidebar, expand the **test widget**, check **Coverage**, and run tests from there — this runs the `storybook` project specifically (so it's the same scope as `test:coverage:storybook` above) and gives you a clickable, interactive coverage report right in the browser, file by file, line by line.

This is entirely free — `@storybook/addon-vitest` and the coverage engine (`@vitest/coverage-v8`) are open source, run locally, no account or usage limits. Nothing to configure; both are already installed and wired into `.storybook/main.ts`.

## Lint & type checks

Not part of the two Vitest projects, but run alongside them in CI:

```bash
npm run lint           # eslint .
npx tsc -b --noEmit    # typecheck, no build output
```

## Token & role governance

Design-system-specific checks — not generic tests, but gate the same way in CI:

```bash
npm run tokens:check          # build + diff + validate + contrast, all in one
npm run roles:check:strict    # fails if any component bypasses getRoleColor()
```

See [Roles](?path=/docs/foundations-roles--docs) for what `roles:check` is actually enforcing, and `docs/foundations/TOKENS.md` for the full token build pipeline.

## What CI actually runs

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on **push to any branch** (not just `main` — broadened so feature branches get real signal instead of nothing until merge) and on **pull requests targeting `main`**:

1. `npm ci`
2. `npm run docs:lint`
3. `npm run lint`
4. `npm run tokens:check`
5. `npm test` — both Vitest projects
6. `npm run build`
7. (PR only) `npm run build-storybook`, uploaded as a downloadable artifact

Two more workflows run the same broadened push trigger: `governance.yml` (strict token/role governance) and `commitlint.yml` (conventional-commit message linting). `contrast.yml` runs on both push and PR, but only when `src/**`, `scripts/check-contrast.js`, `package.json`, or `dist/tokens.json` actually changed — see `.github/workflows/*.yml` for the exact trigger conditions on each.

If a PR-only step (Storybook build artifact) is what you need to check locally before pushing, `npm run build-storybook` reproduces it exactly.

---

# Governance This repo enforces three separate, interlocking governance systems. Each one ...
import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';
import { GovernanceMap, TokenGovernanceFlow, CIGatesFlow, DocPlacementFlow } from './_components/GovernanceFlows';

<Meta title="Foundations/Governance" />

# Governance

This repo enforces three separate, interlocking governance systems. Each one exists to catch a different kind of drift, and each has its own detailed doc — this page is the map between them, with the visual flow each one is missing on its own.

<GovernanceMap />

---

## 1. Token & role governance

**What it protects:** that every color in the codebase traces back to an approved token, through the 3-tier architecture — never a hardcoded hex value.

<TokenGovernanceFlow />

**Needing a new token that doesn't exist yet** is a separate, upstream decision — design/approval, not enforcement. That flow (which layer, who signs off, how long it takes) is fully mapped in **`docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_DECISION_TREE.md`**, with the written process in **`docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_PROCESS.md`**. This diagram is the other half: once a token *does* exist, what stops someone from bypassing it.

### Checked by

| Command | Checks |
|---|---|
| `npm run roles:check:strict` | Any component importing `tokens.*` or `semanticColors.*` directly, a dangling `--role-*` variable, or a hex literal in `src/components/ui/` source |
| `npm run tokens:check` | Token build succeeds, no unauthorized primitive diff, DTCG export valid, WCAG contrast on every enforced pair |
| `npm run governance:ci` | Every gate below, bundled — this is what `governance.yml` runs in CI |

Full architecture, naming rule, and dark-mode mechanics: [Roles](?path=/docs/foundations-roles--docs), [Colors](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs), and **`docs/foundations/TOKENS.md`**.

---

## 1b. The gates that check the gates

**What it protects:** that a green result means something.

Every gate in this repo that has ever been wrong was wrong the same way — it
measured something *adjacent* to what it claimed, and reported green while the
real defect shipped. The axe gate once ran **zero** checks across every story.
The role gate parsed **6 of 55** role names. The registry gate checked index
entries rather than dependency edges. A published release shipped an
`index.d.ts` that did not compile, with all eight gates green.

A green gate is indistinguishable from a disabled one unless something asserts
otherwise. So two harnesses do the asserting, and both run in `governance:ci`.

| Command | Checks |
|---|---|
| `npm run gates:selftest` | Writes a probe containing one real violation per gate, runs the gate, and requires it to exit non-zero **and name the probe**. Exiting non-zero alone is not evidence — a crash, a malformed probe, or an unrelated pre-existing violation all look like a healthy gate |
| `npm run metrics:selftest` | The same idea for the 14 `ds:score` metrics, in **both** directions: a change that should move a metric must move it, and one that should *not* must leave it exactly alone |
| `npm run ds:score` | The health score itself — 14 frozen formulas grouped by goal (development readiness, governance, scalable global system, AI-agent readiness), readable at any git revision so history is backfillable |

The second direction is the one that earns its keep. A metric is a *number*,
and a number can move for the wrong reason: `prop_docs` was once satisfied by
14 docblocks sitting in **empty interface bodies**, which react-docgen cannot
turn into a prop description. The metric moved 44 → 80 while the thing it names
did not budge. Only a probe asserting "this change must *not* count" catches
that.

Adding a gate means adding its probe; adding a metric means adding both of its
probes. That is deliberate friction.

---

## 2. CI quality gates

**What it protects:** that nothing broken — a failing test, a type error, an undocumented token change, a bad commit message — reaches `main`, regardless of which branch it was written on.

<CIGatesFlow />

Push triggers are deliberately **not** `main`-only — this repo does substantial work directly on feature branches, so every branch gets real signal instead of nothing until merge.

**Reproduce any of this locally** before pushing — the exact command for each step is on [Testing](?path=/docs/foundations-testing--docs), and the README's CI & Quality Gates section has the full failure cheatsheet.

---

## 3. Documentation governance

**What it protects:** against exactly what already happened once in this repo — ~70 one-off status reports and build summaries accumulating at the repo root because nothing told anyone where a new doc belonged. `docs:check-sprawl` is the mechanical backstop; the decision ladder below is what actually prevents a new doc from needing to be moved later.

<DocPlacementFlow />

The mechanical gate (`docs:check-sprawl`, run as part of `docs:lint` in every CI run) only catches the literal failure mode — a new `.md` file landing at repo root outside the five allowlisted files. It can't enforce "does an existing doc already cover this" or "has this doc gone stale" — those need judgment, which is what the ladder above is for. Full text version, with the actual list of examples this rule already fixed: **`CLAUDE.md` → Documentation Governance**.

---

## Where each system's detail lives

| System | This page has | Full detail |
|---|---|---|
| Token & role | Enforcement flow | `docs/foundations/TOKENS.md`, `docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_PROCESS.md`, `docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_DECISION_TREE.md` |
| CI gates | Trigger + pipeline flow | [Testing](?path=/docs/foundations-testing--docs), README → CI & Quality Gates |
| Documentation | Decision-ladder flow | `CLAUDE.md` → Documentation Governance, `docs/README.md` |

_This page mirrors `docs/GOVERNANCE.md` (same content, rendered as Mermaid diagrams there for GitHub — this version renders as MDS components so it stays on-brand and theme-aware in Storybook). Keep both in sync if the flows change._

foundations-changelog--docs · ./src/docs/80-Changelog.mdx
# Changelog Every released version of the design system, and what changed in it. This page...
import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';
import { Changelog } from './_components/Changelog';

<Meta title="Foundations/Changelog" />

# Changelog

Every released version of the design system, and what changed in it.

This page renders [`CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/antoniopezzella/marsh-design-system/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)
directly from the repository — it is not a hand-kept copy, so the two can
never disagree. Nothing below is written by hand.

## How entries get here

Entries are generated from **conventional commit messages**, so the commit
you write *is* the changelog entry. There is no separate step to remember,
and no way for a change to ship undocumented as long as it follows the
format.

```
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

feat(components): add a size prop to Badge
fix(theme): repair the border-radius scale
```

`commitlint` enforces this at commit time (see **Foundations → Governance**),
which is why an invalid type, an unknown scope, or a capitalised subject is
rejected before a commit lands.

The `type` decides which section an entry appears under:

| Commit type | Section |
| --- | --- |
| `feat` | Features |
| `fix` | Bug Fixes |
| `perf` | Performance |
| `refactor` | Refactoring |
| `docs` | Documentation |
| `build` | Build System |
| `ci` | Continuous Integration |
| `test` | Tests |
| `chore` | Chores |

Cutting a release runs `npm run release` (standard-version), which reads the
commits since the last tag, works out the next semver number from their
types, writes them into `CHANGELOG.md`, and tags the result.

**Work that has been merged but not yet released does not appear below** —
it lands here on the next release. To see what is currently unreleased,
compare `main` against the latest tag.

import { Modal, Box, Button } from '@mui/material';
import React from 'react';
export function Example() {
  const [open, setOpen] = React.useState(false);
  return (
    <>
      <Button variant="outlined" onClick={() => setOpen(true)}>Open Modal</Button>
      <Modal open={open} onClose={() => setOpen(false)}>
        <Box p={2} sx={{ position: 'absolute', top: '50%', left: '50%', transform: 'translate(-50%, -50%)' }} bgcolor="background.paper">
          Hello from a raw MUI Modal
        </Box>
      </Modal>
    </>
  );
}

<Example />

Story UI/Story Generator

story-ui-story-generator--docs · ./src/stories/StoryUI/StoryUIPanel.mdx
export const StoryUIPanelWrapper = () => ;
{/*
  Story UI Panel - MDX Documentation Page

  This MDX file renders the Story UI Panel as a standalone documentation page.
  Using MDX instead of a .stories.tsx file ensures the React component renders
  correctly across ALL framework Storybooks (React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Web Components).

  Why this works:
  - MDX is processed by @storybook/addon-docs which always uses React
  - Regular .stories.tsx files render in the Preview iframe using the project's framework
  - Non-React frameworks cannot render React components in their Preview
  - MDX pages bypass this limitation by being compiled with React directly

  Port Configuration:
  - The port is automatically read from VITE_STORY_UI_PORT environment variable
  - This is set during `npx story-ui init` and stored in .env
  - URL parameter override: ?mcp-port=XXXX

  Reference: Steve Dodier-Lazaro (Storybook team) recommendation
*/}

import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';
import { StoryUIPanel } from './StoryUIPanel';
import { useEffect, useState, useRef } from 'react';

<Meta title="Story UI/Story Generator" />

export const StoryUIPanelWrapper = () => {
  const [isReady, setIsReady] = useState(false);
  const hasInitialized = useRef(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    // Only run once on mount
    if (hasInitialized.current) return;
    hasInitialized.current = true;

    if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
      // Check for URL parameter override for MCP port
      const urlParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
      const mcpPortParam = urlParams.get('mcp-port');

      if (mcpPortParam) {
        // URL parameter takes highest priority
        window.STORY_UI_MCP_PORT = mcpPortParam;
      }
      // Otherwise, let StoryUIPanel.tsx's getApiBaseUrl() handle port detection
      // from VITE_STORY_UI_PORT environment variable (set during story-ui init)
    }

    setIsReady(true);
  }, []);

  // Don't render until initialized to prevent hydration issues
  if (!isReady) {
    return (
      <div style={{
        display: 'flex',
        alignItems: 'center',
        justifyContent: 'center',
        height: '100vh',
        color: '#666'
      }}>
        Loading Story UI...
      </div>
    );
  }

  return <StoryUIPanel />;
};

{/*
  Full-screen container to match the original story layout.
  The StoryUIPanel component handles its own internal styling.
*/}
<div style={{
  position: 'fixed',
  top: 0,
  left: 0,
  right: 0,
  bottom: 0,
  overflow: 'hidden'
}}>
  <StoryUIPanelWrapper />
</div>
